chief_complaint: inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity, and academic underperformance across home and school environments (ADHD)
hpi_details: 8-year-old boy brought by parents upon recommendation of his 2nd-grade teacher. Teacher reports child constantly squirms in his seat, blurts out answers before questions are completed, interrupts classmates, and fails to finish classwork despite adequate intelligence. Parents note similar struggles at home since kindergarten: cannot follow multi-step instructions, loses his homework, climbs on furniture excessively, and is easily distracted by minor noises. Has no developmental delays or speech problems.
ideas: parents exhausted by daily homework battles and constant hyperactive behavior
concerns: parents worried child will fail school and get labeled as a troublemaker
expectations: want behavioral evaluation and advice on whether stimulant medication is appropriate and safe
pmh: Normal developmental history, normal vision and hearing screens

clinical_knowledge.topic: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Combined Presentation, Moderate evaluation and management
core_concepts: ADHD requires a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, onset before age 12, impairment, and symptoms in at least two settings; use parent and teacher information rather than a single observation.
Screen for learning or language disorders, anxiety, trauma, sleep disorders, sensory impairment, autism, mood symptoms, substance exposure, and medication effects that can mimic or accompany ADHD.
For school-age children, combine parent training and school supports with medication when impairment remains significant; engage the child and caregivers in shared decision-making.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity, and academic underperformance across home and school environments (ADHD)

Key HPI features: 8-year-old boy brought by parents upon recommendation of his 2nd-grade teacher. Teacher reports child constantly squirms in his seat, blurts out answers before questions are completed, interrupts classmates, and fails to finish classwork despite adequate intelligence. Parents note similar struggles at home since kindergarten: cannot follow multi-step instructions, loses his homework, climbs on furniture excessively, and is easily distracted by minor noises. Has no developmental delays or speech problems.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 82, BP 100/64, Weight 28 kg (normal growth parameters). During office visit, child is pleasant, talks excessively, touches clinic instruments impulsively, and has difficulty remaining seated for more than 3 minutes. Standardized Vanderbilt ADHD Diagnostic Parent and Teacher Rating Scales collected from both parents and teacher confirm >= 6 of 9 inattentive symptoms and >= 6 of 9 hyperactive-impulsive symptoms occurring frequently and interfering with learning/social function. Lead screening and sleep study evaluation normal.
Relevant background/PMH: Normal developmental history, normal vision and hearing screens
common_misconceptions: A high activity level in one setting alone establishes ADHD.
Good intelligence or a normal physical examination excludes clinically significant ADHD.
Medication alone replaces parent training, school accommodations, and reassessment for comorbidity.
dangerous_errors: Starting a stimulant without reviewing cardiac history, family history of sudden cardiac death or arrhythmia, blood pressure, pulse, height, weight, sleep, appetite, tics, and current medicines.

Missing suicidal thoughts, self-harm, aggression, psychotic or manic symptoms, abuse, or severe functional deterioration; these require urgent safety assessment and escalation according to local emergency pathways.
Attributing new confusion, fluctuating attention, hallucinations, or autonomic instability to ADHD rather than urgently assessing for delirium, intoxication, or withdrawal.
management_principles: Behavioral intervention: initiate evidence-based Parent Training in Behavior Management (PTBM) and coordinate with school for Classroom Accommodations / IEP or 504 Plan (preferential seating near teacher, extra time on tests, breaking assignments into smaller chunks)

Pharmacotherapy: initiate first-line psychostimulant therapy using a product-specific starting dose (e.g., Concerta 18 mg PO every morning, Ritalin LA 20 mg every morning, or Adderall XR 10 mg every morning)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Before prescribing, assess medical and psychiatric contraindications and follow product-specific dosing; monitor appetite, sleep, growth, blood pressure, pulse, mood, and misuse or diversion risk.
Obtain specialty input when there is concerning cardiac history, diagnostic uncertainty, complex comorbidity, poor response, or serious adverse effects.

reference_soap.subjective: 8-year-old male presenting with pervasive, chronic (>6 months) symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity causing functional impairment across two distinct settings (school and home), classic for ADHD.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 82, BP 100/64, Weight 28 kg (normal growth parameters). During office visit, child is pleasant, talks excessively, touches clinic instruments impulsively, and has difficulty remaining seated for more than 3 minutes. Standardized Vanderbilt ADHD Diagnostic Parent and Teacher Rating Scales collected from both parents and teacher confirm >= 6 of 9 inattentive symptoms and >= 6 of 9 hyperactive-impulsive symptoms occurring frequently and interfering with learning/social function. Lead screening and sleep study evaluation normal.
reference_soap.plan: Multidisciplinary multimodal management: 1. Behavioral intervention: initiate evidence-based Parent Training in Behavior Management (PTBM) and coordinate with school for Classroom Accommodations / IEP or 504 Plan (preferential seating near teacher, extra time on tests, breaking assignments into smaller chunks). 2. Pharmacotherapy: initiate first-line psychostimulant therapy using a product-specific starting dose (e.g., Concerta 18 mg PO every morning, Ritalin LA 20 mg every morning, or Adderall XR 10 mg every morning). Monitor baseline and serial height, weight, blood pressure, and heart rate at follow-up visits.

learning_objectives: Apply DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for ADHD requiring onset before age 12, presence of >=6 symptoms across >=2 environments (home and school), and documented functional impairment
Interpret standardized multi-informant assessment scales (Vanderbilt Parent and Teacher Rating Scales) to confirm cross-situational consistency

Compare stimulant (Methylphenidate and Amphetamine derivatives) vs non-stimulant (Atomoxetine, Guanfacine, Clonidine) pharmacotherapeutic profiles and physiological monitoring protocols (vital signs, growth velocity)
Outline evidence-based educational and classroom accommodations (504 Plan/IEP structure) paired with behavioral parent training

teaching.one_liner: Psychiatric evaluation for patient presenting with inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity, and academic underperformance across home and school environments (ADHD).
red_flags: Suicidal thoughts, self-harm, threats to harm others, severe aggression, abuse concerns, or inability of caregivers to keep him safe
New hallucinations, mania, confusion, fluctuating attention, intoxication, or withdrawal symptoms
Chest pain, fainting, palpitations, known heart disease, or family history of sudden cardiac death before stimulant treatment

must_ask.say: Has he had these problems both at home and at school since he was young?
Does he have trouble finishing his schoolwork, following instructions, or losing things?
Does he squirm in his seat, run around, or blurt out answers before questions are finished?
Has he had any hearing or vision problems, sleep issues, or stressful events that could explain this?
How is this affecting his grades, friendships, and family life?

Has he ever talked about hurting himself or others, seemed unusually sad, fearful, confused, or heard or seen things others do not? Does he have fainting, chest pain, heart problems, tics, sleep or appetite problems, or a family history of sudden heart death?
